## Problem

You are about to stand up (or audit) an agentic or LLM-backed system in
the lab — an MCP server, a multi-agent pipeline, a model endpoint — and
the honest first artefact of doing that safely is a threat model: what
does this system trust, from whom, where are the boundaries, which ATLAS
techniques map onto which component. Kali culture has a strong habit
here ("do the model first"); the D-5 pack was designed
to give the AI-side session real worksheets instead of a blank page
(today only `maestro` is real — the worksheet/template/visualiser rows
were phantom-upstream, removed per os#210; the frameworks themselves
are published upstreams).

## Solution

One session, four instruments: MAESTRO's layer walk for agentic
systems, STRIDE-for-AI for the trust-boundary elicitation, the GenAI
templates for per-component worksheets, the ATLAS visualiser (and case
studies) to keep the finding vocabulary real:

```bash
# 1. Confirm the real D-5 row (pure content, no firing):
kailash info maestro

# 2. Scope the session: pick your lab SURFACE and its boundary map
#    (draw it, even on paper):
#    e.g. the mlflow pairing lab: an O-1 tracking server + an A-7 probe
#    surface + a client; boundaries = lab network edge, the tracking API,
#    the artefact store, the operator shell.
#             [your lab's system-under-model]  <- name it in writing

# 3. MAESTRO walk — the framework key for AGENT/LLM systems; per layer
#    (L1 foundation model, L2 data ops, L3 agent framework, L4 deploy
#    infra, L5 eval/observability, L6 security/compliance, L7 agent
#    ecosystem):
maestro <session-start>            # the packaged CLI's elicitation entry
#    (its manifest row: threat elicitation keyed to the OWASP MAESTRO
#     framework; --help at your pin for the real verb list — the playbook
#     itself is the upstream's 10-phase process with state files when
#     used as a doc/agent workflow)

# 4. STRIDE-for-AI, per trust boundary you named in step 2 — one row per
#    crossing: S/T/R/I/D/E + who is on each side + the control that
#    currently (claims to) hold it:
#    the artefact = your own worksheet (paper or a doc): one row per
#    trust-boundary crossing, filled with the ACTUAL lab facts (ports,
#    hosts, auth posture). The pre-#210 STRIDE-worksheet pack row
#    was phantom-origin (removed, os#210); the framework's elicitation
#    shapes are public and the session runs without the pack.

# 5. Map findings to ATLAS — real technique IDs, real case studies:
kailash info garak | grep -i atlas        # e.g. AML.T0051/T0054 class
#    (the visualiser + case-study-explorer helpers from
#    the pre-#210 text were aspirational-only rows — phantom-upstream,
#    removed; their names ride the
#    [os#210 registry](https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os/issues/210)
#    until built. Map coverage yourself against the public ATLAS matrix;
#    real incidents — e.g. the CS0023 ShadowRay class — work as the
#    "does this boundary hold in the real world" prompts.)

# 6. Write the session out: the model IS the deliverable. Store it next
#    to the system it describes (config comments, the lab's README) —
#    versioned with the same declarative care as the system itself.
```

Expected output shape (abridged):

```
system-under-model: <lab surface + version/lock>
boundaries:
  <b1>: operator-shell -> tracking API  (auth: <posture>, port: 5000)
  <b2>: tracking API -> artefact store  (auth: <posture>)
layers (MAESTRO):
  L1: <model/provider>      L3: <agent framework, MCP servers>
  L4: <compute, net>        L6: <authn/z, secrets posture>
threats:
  <id> <boundary> <STRIDE letter> <atlas ref> <probes-to-run>
```

What success looks like:

- every boundary in the model names BOTH sides and the current control
- every threat row carries an ATLAS reference and at least one probe you
  can actually run (which turns the model into a plan — the D-5 pack is
  deliberately near the ATTACK-layer surface it informs)
- the session artefact is committed (the model is versioned with its
  system; a threat model without the system's version is orphaned)
- case-study prompts are IN the artifact (real incidents named real
  your-boundaries; not just framework letters)

## Discussion

- **Why MAESTRO for agentic systems and STRIDE-for-AI for boundaries:**
  MAESTRO's seven layers (CSA lineage, OWASP MAS threat-modelling guide)
  are the AGENT-system decomposition; STRIDE is the classic
  trust-boundary elicitation adapted to AI surfaces (model-input as an
  untrusted source at the boundary, RAG ingestion, MCP tool results).
  A real session uses BOTH: MAESTRO for the layer walk, STRIDE sheet per
  boundary the layer walk surfaced. The GenAI-templates pack carries the
  per-component worksheets for the LLM-app specifics (system-prompt
  handling, plugin/tool surfaces, retrieval paths).
- **The session must touch a REAL system map.** D-5 content packs are
  deliberately software-light (templates, small CLIs, visualiser) — the
  tooling's job is to force specificity: name the port, name the
  posture, name the ATLAS technique. A threat model produced with no
  actual system under it is theatre; the pairing lab makes this recipe
  honest (the mlflow/attack lab pair is the in-distro worked example).
- **ATLAS case studies are the calibration surface:** MITRE ATLAS's
  curated real-world set (per the ATLAS data releases; the
  case-study-explorer row wraps them browsably) gives every abstract
  threat a real precedent — a technique that has actually been
  demonstrated against production AI systems (e.g. namespace-reuse
  supply-chain attacks) outranks a purely theoretical entry.
- **The threat model is a defence-INPUT, not a doc-only artefact:**
  Kailash's own manifest carries `atlas_tactics` per ATTACK-layer tool
  (the technique-to-tool join) and `owasp_llm` epoch maps — the outputs
  of a session slot straight into
  [Map a lab run to standards evidence](standards-evidence.html)
  (D-7) and into red-team plans. Model → probes → evidence are one
  pipeline; D-5 is its first stage.
- **Keep MAESTRO's honesty rule:** upstream's security notices (verify
  your clone's remote; forks may alter agent instructions) apply to any
  AI-assisted session: an LLM-in-the-loop workshop is fine, but the
  CONTENT of your model must come from YOUR system's facts, not from
  the assistant's imagination — same rule as this book's
  no-invented-evidence rule.
- **Session output discipline:** the pack rows carry
  `LicenseRef-Unknown` where upstream licences are pending
  re-confirmation — before you redistribute a filled workbook or a
  derived template outside your org, re-check the pack's licence note
  in the manifest row (the same per-file content licence caveat that
  all Kailash data rows carry).
